messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Workplace: Workplace, Darkness: Dark spaces, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rohan had been a paramedic for over three decades, and in that time, he had seen his share of traumatic events. But nothing could have prepared him for the day he was exposed to toxic chemicals while responding to an industrial accident. It was a typical chaotic scene - sirens blaring, people shouting, and the acrid smell of chemicals hanging heavy in the air. As he rushed to assist a victim, Rohan's mask malfunctioned, and he inhaled a lungful of noxious fumes. The world around him began to spin, and he stumbled, gasping for breath. The aftermath was a blur, but what followed was a gradual unraveling of his carefully constructed sense of control. At first, it was just the smell of alcohol that would transport him back to that terrible day - the scent of hand sanitizer in hospitals, the whiff of beer at social gatherings. Rohan couldn't understand why something as mundane as a drink could evoke such terror in him, but he knew he had to avoid it at all costs. As time passed, his triggers expanded to include dark spaces and even his own workplace. The very places that were once sources of comfort and purpose now filled him with dread. He began to ruminate about the accident, replaying every detail in his mind, wondering what he could have done differently to prevent it. If only he had checked his mask more carefully, if only he had arrived a minute sooner... The what-ifs swirled in his head like a maelstrom, leaving him breathless and exhausted. Rohan tried to drown out these thoughts by keeping himself constantly surrounded by people. He would attend social gatherings, join community events, and even volunteer for extra shifts at work - anything to avoid being alone with his memories. His friends and family began to notice the change in him, but Rohan just shrugged it off, saying he was "just busy." But there were moments when his carefully constructed facade crumbled. A sudden noise, a glimpse of an ambulance out of the corner of his eye, or even just the faint scent of chemicals on someone's clothes could trigger the full memory, and Rohan would be transported back to that fateful day. The terror he felt was overwhelming - it was as if he was reliving the event all over again. When memories did surface, Rohan found himself unable to cope with the emotions that followed. He would feel overwhelmed, like he was drowning in a sea of anxiety and fear. He began to avoid medical cues altogether - hospitals, ambulances, even routine physical examinations became sources of distress. His wife, Nalini, grew concerned about his increasing withdrawal from daily life, but Rohan just couldn't shake off the feeling that he was walking on thin ice. As the months dragged on, Rohan's relationships began to fray at the edges. He stopped attending family gatherings, citing work commitments or exhaustion. His friends noticed he was distant and preoccupied, always glancing over his shoulder as if waiting for something to pounce. Nalini felt like she was losing her husband, bit by bit. It wasn't until Rohan had a full-blown panic attack at work, collapsing in the ambulance bay, that he finally realized he needed help. As he lay on the hospital bed, surrounded by the very medical cues he had been avoiding for so long, Rohan felt like he was staring into the abyss. He knew he couldn't keep running from his memories forever. What brought him to therapy was a desperate desire to reclaim his life - to be able to walk through a dark room without trembling, to smell disinfectant without being transported back to that terrible day. Rohan wanted to learn how to navigate his triggers, to find a way to calm the terror that threatened to consume him at every turn. Most of all, he longed to reconnect with Nalini and rebuild the life they once shared, free from the shadow of that fateful accident.
